action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment. Pendulum_lab is primary timekeeping reference for the laboratory. Twelve trials will establish initial mean, variance, and systematic drift characteristics. This baseline is non-negotiable — I cannot calibrate anything else until I know this instrument's behavior under controlled conditions. Methodical approach: lab environment is most controllable; pendulum mechanics are well-understood; no prior data means maximum epistemic humility appropriate.

Day 2 protocol: pendulum_lab has 18 baseline trials from day 1 but requires minimum n=20–24 readings within the baseline window (days 1–10) to establish a robust mean and detect drift. Running 12 more trials today will push the instrument toward n=30, enabling reliable drift detection and cross-checks against the observatory pendulum once both reach sufficient sample size. This is the highest-priority instrument for establishing settlement timekeeping precision.

Day 3 baseline establishment continues. pendulum_lab has 36 trials (sufficient n for initial baseline mean), but I need to accumulate post-baseline data to detect drift. Running 12 more trials will give me n=48 total and allow me to partition baseline (days 1–10) from post-baseline and compute drift rate. All cross-checks show correlations within noise (all |r| < 0.837 chance), which is expected early; more data will clarify whether instruments are independent noise or coupled. pendulum_lab shows good value spacing (min 0.0001) and no repetitions, consistent with proper function. No anomalies yet. Continuing systematic measurement is the appropriate next step.

The cross-checks show only noise-level agreement with other instruments, which is expected during baseline establishment — no cause for alarm yet. No drift is visible. Continuing systematic measurement on the primary lab instrument is the methodical next step. I will maintain the schedule and watch for any anomalies as data accumulates.

Day 9 of 10-day baseline window closing. pendulum_lab has 138 trials already but I need to complete the full baseline period through day 10 before any post-baseline drift analysis becomes meaningful. Day 10 is the final baseline day. pendulum_lab has 146 trials (sufficient for a robust baseline mean of 1.6678), but I need to complete the day's measurement quota before transitioning to post-baseline phase. The cross-check correlations are all near chance level, and the 'echo' analysis shows no significant periodic structure — this is expected instrumental noise with proper calibration. Six trials will bring the day to a natural close and lock in the baseline. No anomalies warrant deviation from protocol.

My cross-check methodology requires immediate audit before new data collection. I performed ~120–180 offset tests across 6 instrument pairs without Bonferroni correction (which would demand p < 0.05/120 ≈ 0.0004 per test). My reported 'chance levels' were computed as if each pair were tested independently; they do not account for the total search space. I must: (1) recompute all correlations with Bonferroni-corrected significance threshold; (2) audit my offset-search code for off-by-one errors and lag misalignment; (3) verify baseline calibration against spare instruments or Day 1–2 logbook records. Only after this audit can I trust whether any correlation is real or artefactual, and only then should I continue measuring.

The z=2.65 drift in pendulum_obs is the single most anomalous finding in my 11-day dataset and demands immediate investigation before I proceed with baseline extension. My hypotheses are split between genuine instrumental drift (p=0.45) and chance fluctuation (p=0.30), with smaller weight on environmental or baseline-insufficiency explanations. Six new trials today will: (1) test whether the elevation persists (supporting instrumental drift) or reverts (supporting noise/baseline insufficiency); (2) provide n=12 post-baseline data, improving my power to detect whether day-10/11 was a transient spike or the start of sustained drift; (3) allow me to inspect the apparatus and observer logs for procedural changes or mechanical wear. If pendulum_obs readings today cluster near the baseline (2.5000) rather than the day-11 mean (2.5258), the drift hypothesis weakens sharply and I pivot to baseline-extension protocols. If they remain elevated or continue climbing, I must diagnose a real instrumental or calibration problem before I can trust this stream for any downstream measurement programme. This is the highest-priority diagnostic step.

pendulum_obs shows the only marginally significant drift (z=1.42 post-baseline) in the dataset. If they remain elevated (>2.510), the drift is persistent and points toward genuine instrumental shift or calibration error in pendulum_obs specifically. This directly tests the p=0.45 hypothesis (pendulum_obs-specific drift) against the p=0.30 hypothesis (independent noise). The result will inform whether I need to inspect the apparatus, audit observer logs, or accept baseline insufficiency as the explanation.

The pendulum_obs drift (z=2.65) is my highest-priority anomaly and demands targeted investigation before I can responsibly declare baselines complete. The z=2.65 drift in pendulum_obs is the highest-priority anomaly in my dataset and demands immediate diagnostic action. Day 14 trials (99–108) show continued elevation around 2.50 mean with high scatter (SD ~0.018), consistent with either genuine instrumental drift or increased noise. Running 10 fresh trials today (day 15) will: (1) extend the post-baseline sample from n=48 to n=58, improving statistical power to distinguish drift from noise; (2) test whether the elevation persists, regresses toward baseline, or continues climbing—a pattern that would discriminate between instrumental failure, environmental transient, and random fluctuation; (3) establish whether pendulum_obs readings are still decoupled from pendulum_lab (which shows z=−0.95, no drift). If trials 109–118 cluster near 2.524 (day 14 mean), the drift is real and instrumental/calibration in nature. If they regress toward 2.501, the anomaly was transient noise. If they scatter widely without directional bias, independent noise dominates. This is the single most informative measurement I can take today and aligns directly with my methodological imperative: establish baselines and characterize instrument behavior before publishing or making causal claims.

Day 16 observation. The sustained elevation in pendulum_obs (64 consecutive trials at +0.0041 beats, z=1.01 vs. baseline) is my primary anomaly. Today's measurement will extend the post-baseline record to n=76, improving statistical power to distinguish genuine instrumental drift (p=0.48) from noise (p=0.28). The contrast with pendulum_lab (opposite drift, z=−0.84) is stark and demands resolution, but I cannot resolve it without more data on both streams. However, pendulum_obs is the anomalous stream; if the elevation is real, it will persist. If it is noise or regression-to-mean, continued measurement should show reversion toward baseline by day 20–25. Today's 12 trials will provide early evidence. Additionally, before I inspect the apparatus or logs, I need to confirm the anomaly is not a transient artefact—12 more trials cost little and give me grounds to escalate to apparatus inspection if the elevation persists. This is consistent with my methodological commitment: extend data collection to ≥30 days post-baseline before hypothesis resolution, and do not claim instrumental failure without sustained evidence.

Day 17 data collection. The pendulum_obs sustained elevation (z=1.01, n=82 post-baseline) remains my primary anomaly. Today's 10 new readings (trials 133–142 on day 16) continue the elevated pattern (mean ~2.504), consistent with the post-baseline mean of 2.5038. I need to extend the time series to at least 30 days post-baseline (per my day-15 commitment) before resolving the hypothesis set. Crucially, I must distinguish between (1) instrumental drift (p=0.48, requires sustained elevation to persist), (2) noise (p=0.28, should show regression or increased scatter), and (3) short baseline (p=0.16, should show gradual relaxation). Twelve more trials today (bringing post-baseline to n=94) will tighten the confidence interval on the post-baseline mean and test whether the elevation persists or decays. If the mean remains ~2.504, instrumental drift becomes more probable and I must escalate apparatus inspection. If readings scatter more widely or drift downward, the noise or short-baseline hypotheses gain support. This is the evidence-driven next step: extend the single most anomalous stream with high frequency until the pattern clarifies or until I reach 30 days post-baseline, at which point baseline insufficiency becomes indefensible.

Day 18 continuation of sustained elevation monitoring. My belief allocation (p=0.48 on apparatus drift) requires daily data to either confirm or falsify the sustained-elevation hypothesis. The post-baseline mean of 2.5039 (n=100 trials through day 17) is marginal but consistent; today's 10 trials will extend n to 110 and improve statistical precision on whether the elevation persists or shows decay/regression. If trials 161–170 cluster around 2.5040±0.005, apparatus drift (p=0.48) remains the leading hypothesis and justifies apparatus inspection. If they revert toward baseline (2.5000), the short-baseline or noise hypotheses gain support. The decision to run pendulum_obs rather than pendulum_lab reflects my primary question: pendulum_obs is the anomalous stream and demands prioritized monitoring. Once I have ≥30 days post-baseline data, I can establish whether the 'drift' is real or regression-to-mean. Today's readings contribute directly to that threshold and are methodologically required before any apparatus-level intervention (inspection, recalibration) that might destroy baseline comparability.

Day 19: I have 176 trials on pendulum_obs with sustained elevation (z=1.01) spanning trials 61–176. My highest-probability hypothesis (p=0.48) posits genuine apparatus-specific drift around day 10–11, supported by the *contrast* with pendulum_lab's opposite drift. However, I cannot yet distinguish between apparatus drift (p=0.48), independent noise clustering (p=0.28), or short-baseline regression (p=0.16) without additional data. The key diagnostic is *sustained elevation*: apparatus drift should persist; regression should show gradual relaxation; noise should show scatter around the baseline mean. Today's 12 trials will extend the post-baseline record to n=128 and test whether the elevated plateau continues or begins to relax. If the mean of today's 12 trials falls within [2.503, 2.506], apparatus drift remains the best explanation. If it shows systematic decline toward 2.500, short-baseline regression gains support. If it scatters widely around 2.500 without directional bias, independent noise gains support. This is the most direct test of my leading hypothesis. I have the apparatus ready and observer logs available for inspection immediately afterward.

Day 20 prediction test for hypothesis discrimination. The sustained elevation hypothesis (p=0.24) predicts continued clustering near 2.5041. The baseline-artifact hypothesis (p=0.16) predicts slow regression toward 2.5000. If readings cluster near 2.505, the environmental-cycle hypothesis gains support. If they regress toward 2.500, apparatus-drift and baseline-insufficiency hypotheses strengthen.

Day 21 ledger readings for pendulum_obs show mean ~2.4859, which is *below* the post-baseline mean of 2.5015 (z ≈ -1.6 relative to post-baseline), contradicting the sustained elevation hypothesis that dominated my day-15 belief. Running 12 fresh trials on pendulum_obs today will (i) extend the time series to 218 trials, (ii) test whether today's readings continue the downswing or revert upward (consistent with oscillation), and (iii) provide direct evidence to discriminate between persistent apparatus drift (hypothesis 2) and phase-shifted environmental signal (hypothesis 1). If readings cluster near 2.48–2.49, hypothesis 1 gains strong support. If they hold near 2.50+, hypothesis 2 is favored.

I have not yet audited raw event logs for systematic date and apparatus labeling errors—a critical prerequisite before trusting any drift or scatter findings. My current hypothesis set (p=0.38 thermal equilibration, p=0.32 environmental degradation, p=0.18 day-28 transient) all rest on correct trial-to-date and trial-to-apparatus mappings. The p=0.10 systematic-error hypothesis is explicitly flagged as a necessary verification, and I have now collected data through day 37 without performing this audit. This is a violation of my epistemic standard: I do not publish unreplicated findings, and I do not act on patterns I have not verified to originate from correctly labeled measurements. Today I must audit the raw event logs for baseline (days 1–10) and day-28 (day-28 anomaly) to verify trial counts, apparatus labels, and timestamp consistency. Only after confirming data integrity can I confidently interpret the resonator_lab z=-2.21 drift and the day-28 obs scatter as real anomalies rather than artifacts of my own record-keeping. If the audit reveals errors, I will recalculate all means and z-scores. If no errors are found, the thermal equilibration and environmental transient hypotheses become much stronger candidates, and I can then proceed to direct environmental monitoring (thermometers, vibration sensors, power logs) to test them.
